title: The Arithmetic of Spectra: Factorization, Statistics, and Symmetric Functions
abstract: We study factorizations of the single-particle spectrum of non-interacting quantum systems and their consequences for many-particle statistics. Representing the single-particle partition function by a spectral alphabet, tensor factorizations become multiplicative factorizations of the alphabet, which can be lifted to canonical Bose and Fermi partition functions using standard symmetric-function and $λ$-ring identities. We show how product spectra arise from different factorizations, how antisymmetrization can be assigned across an odd number of factors, and which tensor factorizations are compatible with a fixed spectrum. The paper therefore studies spectral factorization and provides a consolidated combinatorial framework for canonical Bose and Fermi partition functions.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive mathematical framework to study how the factorization of a quantum system's single-particle spectrum determines its many-body statistics. By translating spectral properties into algebraic identities involving symmetric functions, it systematically relates bosonic and fermionic partition functions. The work is significant for providing a unified combinatorial calculus for quantum statistical mechanics.
main_problem: The paper studies the arithmetic structure of spectra, focusing on how factorizations of the single-particle spectrum dictate the resulting many-particle statistics (Bose-Einstein vs. Fermi-Dirac). It aims to provide a unified combinatorial framework for calculating canonical partition functions.
main_result: The bosonic and fermionic statistics are systematically related through spectral factorization identities, which can be mapped onto combinatorial structures like descent sets or occupation matrices. The framework successfully relates product spectra to specific algebraic structures governing the partition functions.
method: The methodology involves representing the spectrum via a formal alphabet and utilizing spectral factorization, connecting tensor factorizations to multiplicative factorizations. Advanced tools include symmetric functions, $\lambda$-rings, and the RSK correspondence to translate spectral properties into combinatorial identities.
model_or_system: The analysis is applied to non-interacting quantum systems, generalizing from the imaginary-time propagator ($e^{- eta H_1}$) to an arbitrary trace-class one-particle kernel. Concrete examples include the harmonic trap and the rectangular infinite well, where the spectrum is separable into multiple sectors.
key_observables: Canonical partition functions ($Z_{n,B}, Z_{n,F}$), the spectral alphabet $X$, and cumulants ($\kappa_j$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($ eta$), dimension ($d$), and the structure of the underlying one-particle kernel $K$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the underlying physical structure can be described by spectral alphabets and their arithmetic operations, though limitations exist regarding the natural infinite spectrum.
figures_summary: The notes detail mathematical relationships (Equations 13, 15, 18, 20, 21) showing how additive and product spectra lead to specific forms for bosonic and fermionic partition functions, and how these relate to combinatorial objects like descent sets.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general framework using spectral alphabets and factorizations for non-interacting systems. It then details the relationship between bosonic and fermionic statistics using symmetric functions and combinatorial tools (like descent sets). Finally, it applies this to specific physical models, such as the harmonic trap, to derive concrete results regarding symmetry and dimensionality.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep mathematical link between spectral theory, combinatorics (symmetric functions), and fundamental quantum statistics, which is highly relevant for understanding correlation functions in many-body quantum systems.
